Let’s dive into Chapter 2: The Twelve Habits That Hold Women Back.
Now that we’ve built some awareness, it’s time to shine a light on the specific habits that can quietly limit our professional growth. Here’s the thing—these aren’t personal flaws or weaknesses. They’re just behaviors we pick up along the way, often shaped by our early experiences and the messages we get from the world around us.
Imagine being able to spot these habits in your own life—almost like finding hidden corners you didn’t know existed. Once you see them, you can actually do something about them. That’s empowering, isn’t it?
So, what are these habits? Well, they usually fall into a few big categories: being reluctant to claim your achievements, waiting for hard work to speak for itself, focusing too much on becoming an expert, building relationships but not really leveraging them, and trying to go it alone without bringing in allies.
Let’s talk about minimizing achievements. Many women grow up hearing that modesty is a virtue. So in the workplace, it’s easy to slip into the habit of downplaying your successes or giving credit to luck or the team, instead of owning your effort. While humility is great, it can mean you’re overlooked when opportunities come up.
Then there’s the idea that hard work will always get noticed. It makes sense—after all, that’s how things usually work in school, right? But in the real world, if you wait quietly for someone to reward your effort, you might get passed over by people who are more comfortable shining a light on their own contributions.
Another habit is overvaluing expertise. It’s easy to believe that if you just become the go-to expert, advancement will follow. But here’s the catch—leadership isn’t just about technical skills. It’s about delegating, influencing others, and seeing the bigger picture. If you only focus on being the expert, you might miss out on those broader opportunities.
And what about relationships? Women are often great at building supportive connections, but sometimes those relationships stay in the “friendly” zone instead of being used strategically. If you’re always the reliable team player, but never the go-to leader, it might be time to start thinking differently about the networks you’ve built.
Finally, a lot of women try to handle everything on their own—maybe out of pride, or maybe because asking for help feels uncomfortable. But the truth is, having mentors, allies, and supporters can make a huge difference in career growth. No one succeeds completely solo.
Let’s make this even clearer. Here are some of the most common habits that can hold women back:
Downplaying achievements or brushing off praise. Waiting for others to notice and reward your hard work. Focusing so much on expertise that you miss out on bigger leadership roles. Building relationships, but not using them to move your career forward. Avoiding self-promotion because you’re worried about seeming boastful. Not asking for support or bringing allies on board. Putting your current job ahead of your career dreams—getting stuck in today’s tasks instead of thinking long-term. Falling into the perfection trap—believing everything has to be flawless. Saying yes to every request because you want to please everyone. Minimizing yourself—shrinking in conversations or using language that makes you seem less important. Ruminating over mistakes or things you wish you’d done differently. And, letting loyalty turn into self-sacrifice—staying somewhere out of obligation, even when it’s holding you back.
Here’s something to keep in mind: these habits make sense. They’ve often been reinforced by cultural messages about how women should behave. But the first step toward changing them is simply recognizing them for what they are—habits, not destiny.
Once you see them clearly, you get to choose. Which ones are helping you—and which ones are you ready to leave behind?
